Title: Which Way Should a Ceiling Fan Turn in Winter?
Description: Most ceiling fans have a small direction switch on the motor housing. In winter, many makers suggest running the fan on low, turning clockwise as you look up, so it gently pulls air up and pushes the warm air near the ceiling back down without a cold breeze. Turn the fan off and let it stop before you flip the switch. Check your fan's manual, since some models differ. More easy seasonal checks on Walter's page.

Title: Dehumidifiers Running at a House Showing? Ask This Question
Description: A dehumidifier humming in the basement during a showing isn't automatically bad, but it's worth a question. Ask the seller why it's there and whether the basement has ever had water. Look for stains low on the walls, white powdery deposits, rust on metal legs and a musty smell, and point them out to your home inspector. More house-hunting red flags on Walter's page.

Title: Your Attic Hatch Could Be the Biggest Draft in the House
Description: The attic hatch or pull-down stairs are often just a loose panel with no seal and no insulation on top, so warm air escapes straight into the attic all winter. Add weatherstripping around the edge where the hatch sits, and insulation on the attic side of the panel. It's a small weekend job that makes a hallway noticeably less drafty. More winter home prep on Walter's page.

Title: Three-Prong Outlets in an Older Home May Not Be Grounded
Description: In older homes, two-prong outlets were sometimes replaced with three-prong ones without adding a ground wire. They look modern but aren't grounded. A simple plug-in outlet tester from a hardware store shows "open ground" on outlets like this. If you find them, have a licensed electrician look at the options. Check what's common for your build year in Walter's free house-age tool.

Title: Clean Your Range Hood Filter Before the Holiday Cooking Starts
Description: Before the big holiday cooking days, look at the filter in your range hood. A greasy filter can't pull smoke, steam and cooking smells out well, and built-up grease near the stove isn't something you want. Most metal mesh filters pop out and wash in hot soapy water; charcoal filters get replaced instead. Check your hood's manual. More quick home checks on Walter's page.

Title: White Powder on Basement Walls (Efflorescence) — What It Means
Description: White, chalky or crusty deposits on basement walls or floors are called efflorescence. They're minerals left behind when water moves through concrete or block and dries on the surface. It doesn't mean the house is bad, but it does mean water has been getting in. Ask about it, check the grading and gutters outside, and have your inspector take a close look. Title: Clean Your Dishwasher Filter (Most People Don't Know It's There)
Description: Many newer dishwashers have a filter at the bottom of the tub, under the lower rack. When it clogs with food bits, dishes come out gritty and the machine can smell. On most models it twists out by hand: rinse it under the tap, scrub gently with a soft brush and lock it back in place. Check your dishwasher's manual for how often. Title: Cast Iron Drain Pipes in an Older Home — What to Look For
Description: Many older homes have heavy black cast iron drain pipes. They can last a long time, but with age they can rust from the inside, crack or leak at joints. Where you can see them in the basement, look for rust flakes, cracks, damp spots and stains. If you're buying, a sewer camera inspection shows the line out to the street. Title: Where Is Your Gas Meter? What Every Homeowner Should Know
Description: If your home has natural gas, know where the meter is and ask your gas company how they want you to handle the shutoff. If you ever smell gas, don't flip switches or use the phone inside: get everyone out, then call the gas company or 911 from outside. Once the gas has been shut off, let the gas company turn it back on and relight things. A simple safety habit. More home safety checks on Walter's page.
Keywords: gas meter shutoff, smell gas what to do, home safety tips, natural gas safety, new homeowner tips, emergency preparedness

Title: Space Heater Safety Checklist — The 3-Foot Rule and More
Description: Before you plug in a space heater this winter: keep anything that can burn at least three feet away, plug it straight into a wall outlet (not an extension cord or power strip), pick a model with tip-over and overheat shut-off, and turn it off when you leave the room or go to bed. Fuel-burning heaters need CO alarms too. Read Walter's full space heater safety guide.
Keywords: space heater safety, space heater tips, winter home safety, fire prevention, winter home prep, home safety checklist

Title: Keep Your Furnace Vent Pipes Clear of Snow This Winter
Description: Many high-efficiency furnaces and water heaters vent through a side wall with two plastic pipes instead of a chimney. If drifting snow, leaves or a bush block them, the appliance can shut down, and a blocked exhaust is a carbon monoxide concern. Find yours now, keep the area clear all winter, and make sure your CO alarms work. More winter home prep on Walter's page.
Keywords: furnace vent pipe snow, high efficiency furnace, winter home prep, carbon monoxide safety, furnace maintenance, homeowner tips

Title: Ask the Seller for 12 Months of Utility Bills Before You Buy
Description: A smart question before you buy a house: can I see the last 12 months of utility bills? Very high heating or cooling months can point to an aging furnace or AC, thin insulation, drafty windows or a leaky attic. Compare them with how many people live there and how they use the house, and bring any questions to your home inspector. More seller questions on Walter's page.
Keywords: questions to ask when buying a house, utility bills, home buying tips, first time home buyer, energy efficient home, house hunting

Title: Check Outdoor Steps and Railings Before Ice Season
Description: Walk every outdoor step and grab every railing before winter: front steps, back deck, porch and basement stairs outside. Loose railings, wobbly treads, rotted wood or crumbling concrete edges are much worse once there's ice. Tighten what you can while it's dry, and have anything structural looked at by a pro. Keep a spot for ice melt and a shovel by the door. More winter checks on Walter's page.
Keywords: outdoor railing safety, porch steps repair, winter home prep, deck safety check, home safety tips, fall home maintenance

Title: Buying an Older Home? Ask About an Old Heating Oil Tank
Description: Many older homes were once heated with oil, and some still have the tank, sometimes buried in the yard. Clues: a small fill pipe or vent pipe sticking out of the ground or a basement wall, or old copper lines in the basement. Ask the seller if there is or was a tank and whether it was removed, with paperwork. Your agent can tell you what's normal locally. Pick your build year in Walter's free house-age tool.

Title: How to Find Drafts in Your House (The Paper Test and More)
Description: Cold spots in the house? Find the drafts with simple tests on a windy day: close a door or window on a sheet of paper and see if it slides out, feel around outlets and trim with a damp hand, and look for light around closed doors. Start with doors, the attic hatch and outlets on outside walls. Read Walter's full guide on finding and fixing drafts.

Title: 6 Home Checks Before Holiday Guests Arrive
Description: Holiday guests on the way? A short home checklist for the week before: test the smoke and CO alarms, clean the range hood filter before the big cooking day, deal with slow drains before the house fills up, make sure steps and walkways are lit, check that the guest room actually gets warm, and keep a clear path to every exit. Title: Low Water Pressure at One Faucet? Clean the Aerator First
Description: If one faucet suddenly has a weak or sputtering stream, check the aerator first: the small screen at the tip of the spout. Unscrew it by hand (or with a cloth-wrapped wrench), rinse out the grit and mineral buildup, and screw it back on. If every faucet in the house is weak, that's a different problem worth asking a plumber about. More easy fixes on Walter's page.

Title: Buying a House in Winter? What Snow Can Hide
Description: Buying a house in winter has upsides, and one catch: snow can hide the roof, the grading, the driveway and the yard. Ask the seller for photos from warmer months, ask about roof age and drainage, and read your inspection report for anything the inspector noted they couldn't see. Winter is also a good time to feel how warm each room stays. More buyer tips on Walter's page.

Title: Does Your Older Home Still Have a Fuse Box? What to Know
Description: Some older homes still have screw-in fuses instead of breakers. A fuse box isn't automatically unsafe, but it may be decades old and sized for far fewer appliances than a house uses today. Never replace a fuse with a bigger one than the circuit is rated for. If you're buying or own a home with fuses, have a licensed electrician check it. Pick your build year in Walter's free house-age tool.

Title: Winter Power Outage? Never Run a Generator Inside the House or Garage
Description: If the power goes out this winter, a portable generator must stay outside, never in the house, garage, basement or crawlspace, even with doors or windows open. Keep it far from windows, doors and vents, and follow the maker's instructions for distance. Have working battery-powered or battery-backup CO alarms. Title: 5 Questions to Ask Your Home Inspector Before You Buy
Description: Go to the home inspection if you can, and ask: what worries you most about this house? What couldn't you see or test today? Which items need a specialist, like a roofer, electrician or sewer scope? What would you fix first? What is close to the end of its life? The answers help you plan and negotiate.
